summary: Defines the Extended Report (XR) packet type for RTCP, the control companion to RTP media streams. XR packets carry report blocks, with seven block types defined here, that convey statistics beyond the basic sender and receiver reports. This helps uses such as voice over IP monitoring. It also describes signaling XR use with SDP.

eli5.summary: When friends play a video call, simple report cards say how things went. This adds a longer, more detailed report card, so people running the call can see exactly what went wrong with the sound or picture.

subtitle: A new RTCP packet type that carries detailed receive statistics and voice-quality metrics beyond the basic reports.

tldr.problem: The basic RTCP Sender and Receiver Reports carry only a small set of statistics. Applications such as multicast network inference and VoIP monitoring need more detailed numbers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3611 defines an Extended Report (XR) RTCP packet, packet type 207, that holds a series of typed report blocks. Seven block types are defined, and an SDP attribute called rtcp-xr tells participants which blocks to use.
tldr.outcome: XR packets supplement existing RTCP packets without changing how the RTCP reporting interval is calculated. New block types can be added later through an IANA registry.

today: RFC 3611 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2003, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself sets up IANA registries for new XR block types and SDP parameters so that further blocks can be added.

sections.title: Why Extended Reports Exist
sections.content:
RTP sessions use RTCP (see RFC 3550) to share simple reception statistics. RFC 3611 defines the Extended Report (XR) packet type, which carries information beyond the reception report blocks of the Sender Report (SR) and Receiver Report (RR). It is not put into profile-specific extensions of SR or RR because the information is useful across RTP profiles. Network management data is one example.

An XR packet holds report blocks, and seven block types are defined. Three give packet-by-packet reports: Loss RLE, Duplicate RLE and Packet Receipt Times. Two deal with reference times: Receiver Reference Time and DLRR. Two are summary blocks: Statistics Summary and VoIP Metrics.

The packet-by-packet blocks were designed with network tomography in mind, such as multicast inference of network characteristics (MINC). The reference time blocks were conceived for receiver-based TCP-friendly multicast congestion control. The VoIP Metrics block is specific to voice applications.

XR packets may be stacked with other RTCP packets into compound packets. They count as RTCP packets for bandwidth calculations, and they do not change the rules for calculating the RTCP reporting interval.
sections.eli5: Normal RTCP reports are short notes about how a call is going. XR adds longer, more detailed notes for people who want to look closely, like a doctor ordering extra tests.

sections.title: The XR Packet and Block Framework
sections.content:
An XR packet has a header of two 32-bit words followed by zero or more report blocks. The header is laid out like other RTCP packets: version (2 bits, value 2), padding (1 bit), 5 reserved bits, a packet type of 207, a 16-bit length and the 32-bit SSRC of the packet's originator. Because of this layout, receivers that do not recognize XR can still parse past it using the length field.

Every report block starts with an 8-bit block type (BT), an 8-bit type-specific field and a 16-bit block length. The length counts 32-bit words minus one, and a block is always a whole number of 32-bit words. A receiver can use the type to demultiplex blocks and the length to find the next block, even when it does not know a block type. An implementation SHOULD ignore incoming blocks whose types are unknown or not relevant to it.

The block type namespace is managed by IANA under the Specification Required policy of RFC 2434. The RFC registers packet type 207 for XR, and the BT value 255 is reserved for future extensions. Future specifications SHOULD avoid BT value 0, because an all-zeros field is often found in an ill-formed packet.
sections.eli5: Every extra page in the report has a label saying what kind of page it is and how long it is. Someone who does not know that kind of page can read the label and skip right over it.

sections.title: Per-Packet Reports and Run-Length Encoding
sections.content:
The Loss RLE block (BT=1) reports, for one RTP source, a trace of one value per sequence number: 1 means a packet with that number was received, 0 means a loss. Because a raw trace is long, it is compressed with run-length encoding into 16-bit chunks. A run-length chunk describes between 1 and 16,383 identical events, a bit-vector chunk describes 15 mixed events, and an all-zero null chunk pads the block to a 32-bit boundary. A null chunk MUST appear at the end if the number of other chunks is odd, and in no other place.

To keep reports small, the block supports thinning. A thinning value T from 0 to 15 selects only those packets whose sequence numbers are multiples of 2^T. With T=0 every packet is reported on, and with T=15 one in every 32,768 packets is reported on. The choice of T is left to the application. A Loss RLE block MUST NOT cover a range of 65,534 or more sequence numbers.

The RFC asks reporters to favor accuracy over interpretation. A participant SHOULD NOT require a minimum number of packets before reporting on a sender, and SHOULD treat all sequence numbers as valid. Rollover of the 16-bit number is judged by placing each new number no more than 32,768 packets ahead of or behind the most recent one, whichever is closer.

The Duplicate RLE block (BT=2) has the identical format, but 0 means duplicates were seen for that number and 1 means none were. The Packet Receipt Times block (BT=3) lists a 32-bit receipt time for each reported sequence number, in the same units as the RTP timestamp. Every number reported MUST have been received at least once, and if duplicates arrived at different times, only the earliest time may be reported.

Even with run-length encoding, per-packet blocks can use bandwidth out of proportion to normal RTCP packets, so the RFC advises caution in sending them.
sections.eli5: Imagine writing down for each page of a book whether it arrived. Instead of writing a long list, you say that the first 21 pages arrived, which is shorter. Thinning means you only check every fourth page to make the note even smaller.

sections.title: Round-Trip Time and Summary Statistics
sections.content:
The Receiver Reference Time block (BT=4) lets a receiver that is not an RTP sender share a 64-bit NTP wallclock timestamp. Another participant can answer with a DLRR block (BT=5), which contains for each receiver the last RR timestamp (LRR) and the delay since that block was received (DLRR), in units of 1/65536 seconds. The original receiver records the arrival time A of the DLRR and computes the round-trip time as A - LRR - DLRR. This extends the SR and DLSR mechanism of RTCP to participants who are not senders.

The Statistics Summary block (BT=6) reports summary numbers for a sequence number interval. Flag bits say which fields are reported: lost packets (L), duplicate packets (D), jitter (J) with minimum, maximum, mean and deviation, and a two-bit TTL or Hop Limit flag (ToH) where 1 means IPv4 TTL, 2 means IPv6 Hop Limit and 3 MUST NOT be used. Fields for unreported items MUST be present but set to zero, and a receiver MUST ignore a block with a non-zero value in a field flagged as unreported. The block length is the constant 9.

If every receiver sent Receiver Reference Time blocks, a sender might send as many DLRR sub-blocks as there are receivers. The RFC therefore says an application should use discretion about which participants send these blocks and how often.
sections.eli5: To find out how long a letter takes, you send a note with the time on it, and your friend replies saying how long they held it before answering. You subtract the waiting time and what is left is the travel time.

sections.title: VoIP Metrics
sections.content:
The VoIP Metrics block (BT=7, block length 8) is for monitoring voice over IP calls. It applies to any one-to-one or one-to-many voice application that uses RTP and RTCP. Implementations MUST provide values for all of its fields, using the specified default or unknown value when something cannot be measured.

The block separates packets lost on the network from packets the receiver discarded in its jitter buffer, because both hurt call quality equally but have different causes. The loss rate and discard rate are 8-bit fixed-point fractions, computed by dividing by packets expected, multiplying by 256 and capping at 255.

Burst and gap metrics describe how losses cluster. A burst is a stretch that starts and ends with a lost or discarded packet and contains no run of Gmin or more consecutively received packets. A gap is a period of low loss between bursts. A Gmin of 16 is RECOMMENDED, and it MUST NOT be zero or change during an RTP session. Burst and gap density and duration are reported, with durations in milliseconds.

Other groups of fields cover delay (round trip delay and end system delay, in milliseconds), signal level, noise level and residual echo return loss, and receiver configuration such as packet loss concealment and jitter buffer settings. Quality scores include the R factor (an integer from 0 to 100, where 94 is toll quality and 50 or less is regarded as unusable) and mean opinion scores MOS-LQ and MOS-CQ (integers from 10 to 50, equal to MOS times 10). The value 127 means a parameter is unavailable.

Conversational metrics such as the R factor and MOS-CQ are not defined for applications other than simple two-party calls, so they should be reported as unavailable in multicast conferencing.
sections.eli5: This is a detailed health check for a phone call over the internet. It records how many words went missing, how long the delay was, and gives the call a score, like a grade on a report card.

sections.title: Signaling XR Use with SDP
sections.content:
XR blocks MAY be used without prior signaling. For applications configured at session start, the RFC defines an SDP attribute, rtcp-xr, usable at session or media level (a media-level setting replaces a session-level one). It works with the offer/answer model of RFC 3264 and with SDP (RFC 2327) used alongside SAP or RTSP. Participants that do not implement XR ignore the attribute.

Parameters come in two kinds. Unilateral parameters cover blocks that just report on the stream: pkt-loss-rle, pkt-dup-rle, pkt-rcpt-times, stat-summary and voip-metrics. The first three may carry a maximum block size in octets, which means thinning should be applied to meet it. Collaborative parameters involve more than one party; the only one is rcvr-rtt, with mode all or sender, which governs the Receiver Reference Time and DLRR pair.

When the attribute is present, participants SHOULD NOT send XR blocks other than those named, and an attribute with no parameters means no XR blocks should be sent. In offer/answer, the interpretation depends on the direction attribute (sendonly, sendrecv or recvonly). For multicast streams, an offer of a collaborative parameter SHOULD say which participants are to respond, to avoid consuming undue bandwidth.

IANA creates a registry of RTCP XR SDP parameters. New parameters are added under the Specification Required policy.
sections.eli5: Before a call starts, each side can say which extra reports it wants, like asking a teammate to send only the stats you care about. If you say nothing, you get none of the extras.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
XR reports are more detailed than standard RTCP reports, which raises confidentiality concerns. The per-packet blocks make multicast inference of network characteristics possible, which can reveal the rough topology of a multicast tree and path loss rates and delays. This might be sensitive to autonomous system administrators. The VoIP Metrics block makes call quality information available in a standard format, and so more available to eavesdroppers.

The RFC adds no confidentiality mechanism. Encryption such as Secure RTCP can be used by end hosts, but doing so denies monitoring information to third parties such as service providers that carry the calls. As a default, XR packets should not be encrypted or filtered.

Large per-packet blocks also make certain denial of service attacks easier. Because RTCP adjusts its bandwidth automatically, large packets from some participants lengthen the reporting interval for everyone. Applications SHOULD place an upper limit on XR block sizes, and thinning allows the packet-by-packet blocks to meet a size limit.
sections.eli5: Detailed reports can tell snoopers more about your call and your network. Very large reports can also slow everybody down, so the rules say to keep reports to a sensible size.
